lessons.title: Lesson text — Morning Walk (p. 8-10)
lessons.notes_html:
Ahmed lives in Quetta. One day, he woke up very early in the morning. The sky was soft and light grey and a cool breeze was blowing. He got out of bed, brushed his teeth and washed his face. Then he put on his tracksuit and joggers. His mother gave him a bottle of water and reminded him to be careful while crossing the road. The night before, Ahmed had told his cousin Zain that he would go for a morning walk. So, early in the morning, Zain came to Ahmed's house. As Ahmed stepped outside, he saw Zain waiting at the gate with a smile. 'Let's go together!' said Zain happily. The road was almost empty. A few men were walking or riding bicycles. They could see tiny drops of dew on the grass and the leaves. Ahmed and Zain talked and laughed as they walked to Jinnah Park, which was just a few minutes away from their home. When they reached the park, they were happy to see green trees and flowers all around. A gardener was watering the trees and plants. The boys removed their shoes and walked on the soft, wet grass. It felt cold and tickled their toes. After walking and playing for about fifteen minutes, they sat under a tree and drank some water. Zain saw a butterfly and tried to chase it. Ahmed laughed and ran after him. They both felt full of energy and very fresh. Soon, it was time to go back. Zain said goodbye to Ahmed at the street corner near their homes and waved with a smile. He turned towards his house, feeling cheerful after the walk. When Ahmed returned

home, his mother had prepared a healthy breakfast of paratha, an egg and a glass of milk. Ahmed washed his hands and had his breakfast. Ahmed had learnt that morning walk is good for health, gives us energy and keeps our mind fresh. He decided to wake up early every day and enjoy a morning walk.

lessons.title: Grammar — Noun: Types of a Noun (p. 15-17)
lessons.notes_html: Noun is the name of a person, place, animal or thing, e.g., Ali, city, cat, pen, etc. 1. Common Nouns: refer to general, non-specific people, places, things, or animals, etc. Examples: teacher, doctor, player, city, park, school, book, table, car. Sentences: (i) The teacher helped the students with their homework. (ii) The city was full of buildings. (iii) We go to school daily. 2. Proper Nouns: the proper names of people, places, or things etc. and are always capitalized. Examples: Mujtaba, Ali, Ziarat, Chiltan, Askri-Park, Book. Sentences: (i) She is going to visit Karachi next summer. (ii) Mujtaba is my elder brother. (iii) I like English Book. 3. Countable Nouns: nouns that can be counted. Examples: apple - apples, cat - cats, book - books. Sentences: (i) Singular: I ate an apple for a snack. (ii) Plural: The cats chased each other around the garden. 4. Uncountable Nouns: nouns that cannot be counted. Examples: water, sugar, rice, love, advice. Sentences: (i) Please pass me a glass of water. (ii) His advice was very helpful. (iii) I like rice. 5. Collective Nouns: refer to groups of people or things as a single entity. Examples: team, family, class, herd, flock, bunch. Sentences: (i) The team celebrated their victory with a party. (ii) I have a small family. (iii) She picked a bunch of flowers from the garden.

lessons.title: Sentence Structure — Subject and Predicate (p. 30)
lessons.notes_html: Subject: The subject is who or what the sentence is about. It tells us the main person, animal, thing, or idea that the sentence is talking about. Example: The cat sleeps - 'cat' is the subject. Predicate: The predicate tells us what the subject is doing or what is happening to the subject. It usually includes the verb and other words that give more information about the action. Example: The cat sleeps - 'sleeps' is the predicate. Subject and predicate examples: 1. The dog (Subject) - barks loudly (Predicate). 2. The sun (Subject) - shines brightly in the sky (Predicate).

lessons.title: S + V (Subject and Verb) pattern (p. 30-31)

Who or what performs the action of the verb, is the subject. The verb is the word that expresses what that action is. Whoever or whatever receives that action, is the object.

lessons.title: Lesson text — The Woodpecker (p. 39)
lessons.notes_html: There are many beautiful birds in the world and one of them is 'woodpecker'. The woodpecker is an interesting bird. It is found in different colours and sizes. It has a strong, pointed beak that acts as a hammer to remove bark (tough material that covers the outside of a tree) from trees and find insects to eat. It has a long tongue, two to four inches long, that is sticky on the tip for catching insects. Most birds have one toe pointing back and three pointing forward on each foot. Woodpeckers are a little bit different. They have two sharp claws pointing back and two sharp claws pointing forward on each foot to help them hold on to the sides of trees. The life span of a woodpecker is 4-11 years (National Wildlife Federation). Their favourite foods are insects, fruit and nuts. These interesting birds live in forests and wooded areas with lots of trees. Woodpeckers can be found all over the world, except Australia. Picture labels: beak, front claws, back claws.

Indefinite Articles (a, an): 'A' or 'An' is called indefinite articles because it

lessons.title: Grammar — Subjective, Objective and Possessive Pronouns (p. 57-58)
lessons.notes_html:
Subjective Pronouns: Subjective pronouns are used as the subject of a sentence. They perform the action of the verb or specify who or what is doing the action. e.g. I, you, he, she, it, we, they. Examples: 1. I am going

to the store. 2. You are my best friend. 3. He likes to play soccer. 4. She is reading a book. 5. We are going to the beach. Objective Pronouns: Objective pronouns are used as objects of verbs or prepositions. They receive the action of the verb or show the relationship between the verb and other words in the sentence, e.g. me, you, him, her, it, us, them. Examples: 1. She gave him a book. 2. Please pass the salt to me. 3. They invited us to the party. 4. I saw them at the store. 5. He loves his parents. (Note: the book lists 'his' under objective pronouns in example 5 - 'his' is a possessive word, not an objective pronoun, flagged; the same point was flagged in Grade 2.) Possessive Pronouns: Possessive pronouns indicate ownership or possession. They show that something belongs to someone or something else, e.g. mine, yours, his, hers, its, ours, theirs. Examples: 1. The car is mine. 2. Is this pen yours or mine? 3. The cat licked its paws. 4. The house is theirs. 5. The book is hers.

lessons.title: Lesson text — My Beautiful Country Pakistan (p. 65-67)
lessons.notes_html:
My beautiful country, Pakistan, is very special to me. It is in South Asia.

Pakistan is a beautiful country. Let's learn about the different provinces, people, languages, games, culture, and amazing places to visit. Provinces of Pakistan: Pakistan has four provinces: Punjab, Sindh, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa and Balochistan. Punjab: Punjab is known for its green fields where farmers grow important crops like wheat and rice. You can see large farms all over the land. The people of Punjab love delicious food and enjoy playing cricket, kabbadi and hockey. Punjab is home to big cities like Lahore, Faisalabad, Multan, and Rawalpindi. Lahore is full of history and has beautiful buildings like the famous Badshahi Mosque and Shahi Qilla. Sindh: Sindh is full of rich culture and history. You can visit the ancient city of Mohenjo-Daro, which is a very old city! The people of Sindh love to wear their traditional ajrak and Sindhi topi. Big cities like Karachi and Hyderabad are situated in Sindh. You can visit the Mazar-e-Quaid in Karachi where Quaid-e-Azam is buried. Khyber Pakhtunkhwa: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa has tall, snowy mountains and beautiful green valleys. You can see children in traditional Peshawari dress, smiling and playing. The famous Khyber Pass is also found here. Big cities here include Peshawar, Swat, and Dera Ismail Khan. The people are known for being very brave and friendly. Balochistan: Balochistan is the largest province of Pakistan. It has large deserts, high mountains, and beautiful places like the Ziarat Residency and the seaside city of Gwadar. The main cities of Balochistan are Quetta, Gwadar, and Khuzdar. The people of this province are kind, strong and friendly. Languages: Urdu is the national language of Pakistan, but other languages like Punjabi, Sindhi, Pashto, Balochi, Brahvi etc., are also spoken. Games: Pakistan is a country where people love to play different games. People enjoy playing cricket, football, hockey, and badminton. Hockey is the national game of Pakistan. Many people also like traditional games such as kabaddi and gullidanda. Handicrafts:

Pakistan is famous for its beautiful handicrafts. You can find delicate pottery in Multan, colorful embroidery in Karachi, beautiful woodwork in Swat, Balochi embroidered dresses, caps and shawls in Balochistan, and soft carpets in Peshawar. Festivals: We celebrate different cultural festivals like Eid, Independence day, Christmas and Holi. On these days people wear beautiful dresses and enjoy yummy food. Places to Visit: In Pakistan, there are many amazing places to visit! You can explore the ancient ruins of Mohenjo-Daro in Sindh, go hiking in the beautiful valleys of Swat in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, visit the stunning beaches of Gwadar in Balochistan, or see the historic Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, Punjab.

lessons.title: Lesson text — The Importance of Cleanliness (p. 78-80)
lessons.notes_html:
Cleanliness is very important for keeping ourselves healthy and our world beautiful. When we talk about cleanliness, we mean making sure everything around us is neat, tidy, and free from dirt and germs. Let's learn why cleanliness is so important and how we can keep our surroundings clean. Cleanliness Matters: Firstly, cleanliness helps us stay healthy. When we keep our body clean by washing our hands, taking bath, and brushing our teeth, we can prevent germs from making us sick.

Cleanliness also keeps our homes and schools safe and comfortable places to be. Imagine how bad it would be if there were trash and dirt everywhere. Keeping Our Surroundings Clean: There are many simple things we can do to keep our surroundings clean. One important thing is to always throw our trash in the proper bins. We can have separate bins for different kinds of waste, like paper, plastic, and food scraps, and make sure to put our trash in the right one. Another way to keep our surroundings clean is to pick up litter when we see it. If we see trash on the ground, we can pick it up and throw it away in trash bin. Cleaning Up After Ourselves: It is also important to clean up wherever we go. If we make a mess while eating, we can use napkins to wipe up spills and crumbs. After playing with toys or games, we can put them back where they belong instead of leaving them scattered around. By cleaning up, we show respect for our belongings and the people around us. Taking Care of Nature: We should also take care of nature by not littering and by helping to keep parks, playgrounds, and other outdoor spaces clean. When we visit these places, we can make sure to pick up any trash we see and dispose it off properly. We can also help by planting trees and flowers, which make our environment cleaner and more beautiful. We can say that cleanliness is very important for keeping ourselves healthy and our world clean. By practicing good hygiene, keeping our surroundings clean, and taking care of nature, we can all do our part to make the world a better place. So let's remember to always stay clean and tidy, both for ourselves and for our planet.

lessons.title: Story text — The Tale of Honest Hannah (p. 107-108)
lessons.notes_html:
Once upon a time, in small village between green hills and winding rivers, there lived a girl named Hannah. She was known for her bright smile and kind heart. But there was one thing about Hannah that made her special and that was she never told lies. She believed that honesty is the best policy, and she always tried to speak the truth, no matter what. Her friends admired her honesty and often came to her for advice and support. One sunny morning, as she was walking through the village square, she saw a shiny red apple lying on the ground. Curious, she picked it up and looked around to see if anyone had dropped it. But there was no one in sight. She knew that the apple didn't belong to her, so she decided to take it to the village market and ask if anyone had lost it. As she walked through the bustling market stalls, she noticed a little boy crying. 'What's wrong?' she asked gently. 'I lost my favorite apple,' The

boy sniffled. 'I was saving it for a special treat.' Hannah's heart went out to the boy. 'Is this your apple?' she asked, holding out the shiny red fruit. The boy's eyes lit up with joy as he took the apple from Hannah's hand. 'Yes, that's it! Thank you so much!' he exclaimed, and said thank you aloud. She smiled and waved goodbye to the boy before continuing on her way. As she walked, she thought about how good it felt to be honest and help someone in need. She knew that speaking the truth was always the right thing to do, even when it was hard. From that day on, Hannah continued to live her life with honesty and integrity. And though she faced many challenges along the way, she always stayed true to herself and never told a lie. And so, the villagers of the little village came to admire and respect Hannah even more, for she was not only brave and kind but also honest and shining example for all to follow.

lessons.title: Lesson text — Boys and Girls Are Equally Important (p. 122-123)
lessons.notes_html:
Once upon a time, in a small house there lived a brother and sister named Sami and Laiba with their family. Sami was full of energy and loved to play with his toy cars and build towering block towers, while Laiba was kind-hearted and enjoyed dressing up her dolls and arranging tea parties. One sunny afternoon, their parents decided to host a special event to teach them about the importance of equality. As the event began, Sami walked proudly with his chest out, saying he was better at everything than Laiba. 'I'm the best at racing cars and building tall towers. Girls can not do that' he exclaimed proudly, while Laiba looked on with a sad expression. Their father noticed Sami's behavior and gently called him over. 'Sami, come sit with me for a moment' he said,

motioning for Laiba to join them as well. As they sat down, their father began to speak. 'Sami, Laiba, I want to talk to you both about something very important,' he started. 'You see, boys and girls are like two sides of the same coin. Each of you is special and unique in your own way, and neither is better than the other.' Sami looked confused, while Laiba nodded in agreement. Their father continued, 'Sami, just because you are a boy does not mean you are better than Laiba. And Laiba, just because you are a girl does not mean you are not as good as Sami. Boys and girls are equal, and it is important to treat each other with kindness, respect, and love.' Sami's eyes widened as he realized the truth of his father's words. 'But Father, I did not mean to make Laiba feel bad,' he said quietly. 'It's okay, Sami,' their father spoke softly. 'We all make mistakes sometimes. What's important is that we learn from them and try to do better next time.' From that day on, Sami and Laiba made a promise to each other and their parents to always treat each other with kindness and respect, knowing that boys and girls are equal and deserving of love and acceptance. And so, as the event came to a close, Sami and Laiba shook hands, grateful for the lesson they had learned about the importance of equality. And as they played together, they knew that they were different, they would always be equal in each other's eyes.

lessons.title: Fact, Fiction and Non-Fiction (p. 136-137)
lessons.notes_html:
Fact: A fact is a statement that can be proven to be true or false through evidence or observation. Example: The Earth orbits the Sun. This is a fact because it can be confirmed through scientific observation and research. Fictional Text: Fictional text refers to written works that present imagined or invented stories, characters, and events. Non-fiction Texts: Non-fictional text refers to written works that present factual information, real events, and actual experiences. Types of Fictional and Non-Fictional Texts: Fictional Texts - Fictional texts are stories that are made up from someone's imagination. They are not real. Here are three common types: 1. Novels: Example: Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone, is a long story with many characters and chapters that follow Harry's magical journey. 2. Short Stories: Example: The Thirsty Crow is a short story with a beginning, middle, and end, that focuses on one main event. 3. Fairy Tales: Example: Cinderella is a magical story of a kind girl. Non-Fictional Texts - Non-fictional texts are books or articles that are about real people, real places, or real things. Here are three important types: 1. Biographies: Example: The Story of Abdul Sattar Edhi is a book that talks about the life and work of a real person. 2. Informational Texts: Example: A book about plants gives scientific facts, has pictures, diagrams, and headings. 3. News Articles: Example: A newspaper report about a school event tells what happened, where, when, and includes quotes from

people.

lessons.title: Poetic Devices (p. 138-139)
lessons.notes_html: Poetic devices are special tricks that poets use to make poems more fun to read and listen to. Read the Poem aloud: 'A Walk in the Garden' (Edited for Clarity) - I walk in the garden at the break of day, / Birds are singing in a cheerful way. / Flowers bloom in red and blue, / The sky above is bright and true. / I walk, I walk, I walk some more, / Past the tree and by the door. / The sun is like a golden ball, / Shining gently over all. Poetic devices in the Poem: 1. Rhyme and Rhythm - Rhyme is when words at the end of a line sound the same. Rhythm is the beat of the poem. Examples: day / way; blue / true; more / door; ball / all. 2. Repetition - Repetition is when a word or a line is repeated. Examples: 'I walk, I walk, I walk some more'. 3. Simile - A simile compares two different things using the words 'like' or 'as'. Examples: 'The sun is like a golden ball'. 4. Sensory Images - Sensory images are words that help us see, hear, smell, or feel things in the poem. Examples: Hear: 'Birds are singing'; See: 'Flowers bloom in red and blue'; 'The sun is like a golden ball'.

lessons.title: Grammar — Modal Verbs (p. 141-142)
lessons.notes_html:
Modal verbs are auxiliary verbs used to express various degrees of necessity, possibility, ability or permission in a sentence. 1. Should/Should not: Should indicates advice, recommendation, or obligation. Example: You should wear a helmet when riding a bike. Should not indicates prohibition or advice against doing something. Example: You should not play on road. 2. Could/Couldn't: Could indicates ability, possibility, or past ability. Example: She could swim when she was younger. Couldn't indicates inability or impossibility. Example: He couldn't attend the class because he was sick. 3. Must/Mustn't: Must indicates strong obligation, necessity, or certainty. Example: You must submit your assignment by Friday. Mustn't indicates prohibition or strong

advice against doing something. Example: You must not tell a lie. 4. Can/Cannot: Can indicates ability, possibility, or permission. Example: She can speak English fluently. Cannot indicates inability or prohibition. Example: You cannot enter without permission. 5. May/May not: May indicates permission, possibility, or likelihood. Example: You may leave early if you finish your work. May not indicates prohibition or uncertainty. Example: You may not use your phone during the exam.

lessons.title: Lesson text — Eid-ul-Fitr: A Celebration of Joy and Renewal (p. 147-148)
lessons.notes_html:
Eid-ul-Fitr is a very special festival for Muslims. Eid-ul-Fitr comes after the month of Ramadan on the first day of Shawal every year. During Ramadan, Muslims try to be patient, kind, and helpful. They avoid bad habits and try to do good deeds. People prepare for Eid celebrations. Many families clean their homes, buy new clothes, and decorate their houses. The night before Eid is called Chand Raat. People go to markets. Everyone feels excited for the Eid day. On Eid morning, people greet each other with happy smiles. Families visit their relatives, neighbors, and friends. Everywhere you go, people are saying 'Eid Mubarak!' It is a day full of joy and togetherness. Many families cook special food at home. Some families share food with their neighbors. This shows love and kindness in the community. Children enjoy wearing their new clothes and meeting their cousins and friends. They play games and have fun for the whole day. Eid is a reward from Allah for the Muslims. It reminds Muslims to continue good habits even after Ramadan. It teaches them to care for

others, forgive people, and stay thankful. Eid also teaches the importance of family. Spending time with parents, grandparents, brothers, sisters, and friends brings happiness. It helps everyone feel close to each other. Eid is not only about eating and having fun. It is also about sharing. Muslims give Fitrana before the Eid prayer. This money is used to help poor people. Many people also give charity, clothes, and food to those in need. When everyone shares, everyone can enjoy Eid. This makes the festival more meaningful. Festivals bring color and joy to our lives. They give us a chance to meet people, celebrate traditions, and enjoy special moments. People in Pakistan belong to different religions. Muslims celebrate Eid, Christians celebrate Christmas, Hindus celebrate Diwali, and Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi. Pakistan is a beautiful country with people from different religions. We should respect each other's festivals. In this way, we can make our country peaceful and strong.

lessons.notes_html: A descriptive paragraph is a type of writing that uses words to paint a picture in the reader's mind. lessons.title: Lesson text — Media as a Source of Learning (p. 159-160)

Media is a powerful tool for learning, and by exploring books, videos, websites, and games, we can expand our knowledge, creativity, and become dedicated learners. lessons.title: Grammar — Future Tense (p. 164)
lessons.notes_html: Future Tense: Subject + will/shall + first form of the verb + object. Examples: 1. I will go to the library tomorrow. 2. My friends will come to my home tomorrow. 3. You will get first position in exam. 4. I shall meet you at the park at 3 p.m. Will/Shall: To form the future tense with 'will,' we use 'will' followed by the first form of the verb. 'Shall' is less commonly used in modern English for future tense but can still be used for suggestions, offers, or promises. It's mainly used with 'I' and 'we' subjects. 2. Be going to: To form the future tense with 'be going to,' use the appropriate form of the verb 'to be' (am/is/are) followed by 'going to' and then the first form of the verb. Subject + am/is/are + going to + first form of the verb + object. Examples: 1. My parents are going to attend the concert. 2. I am going to visit my uncle next weekend. 3. We are going to have a party on Saturday.

lessons.title: Phrases and Sentences (p. 165-166)
lessons.notes_html: Phrase: A phrase is a group of words that express a single idea or concept, but it does not contain a subject and a verb, so it does not express a complete thought or make sense on its own. Examples: 1. on the table, 2. under the bed, 3. running fast, 4. in the morning, 5. across the street. Sentence: A sentence is a group of words that contains a subject and a verb (predicate), and it expresses a complete thought or idea. Sentences can stand alone and make sense by themselves. Examples: 1. I like to play with my doll. 2. She reads books everyday. 3. They go to the park on Sundays. 4. He eats lunch at noon. 5. Birds fly in the sky. 6. The sun shines brightly.
